docs.title: MLArray
docs.text:
tl;dr: Working with large medical or scientific images for machine learning? -> Use MLArray.

MLArray is a purpose-built file format for N-dimensional medical and scientific array data in machine learning workflows. It replaces the usual patchwork of source formats and late-stage conversions to NumPy/Zarr/Blosc2 by layering standardized metadata on top of a Blosc2-backed storage layout, so the same files work reliably across training, analysis, and visualization tools (including Napari and MITK).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You can install mlarray via pip: 

pip install mlarray

To enable the mlarray_convert CLI command (conversion with MedVol 1.0 or newer), install MLArray with the extra dependencies: 

pip install mlarray[all]

docs.title: Documentaion
docs.text: See the documentation for the API reference, the metadata schema, usage examples or CLI usage.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Below are common usage patterns for loading, saving, and working with metadata.

docs.title: Default usage
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((128, 256, 256))
image = MLArray(array)  # Create MLArray image
image.save("sample.mla")

image = MLArray("sample.mla")  # Loads image

docs.title: Memory-mapped usage
docs.text:
from mlarray import MLArray
import numpy as np

# read-only, partial access (default)
image = MLArray.open("sample.mla", mmap_mode='r')  
crop = image[10:20, 50:60]  # Read crop

# read/write, partial access
image = MLArray.open("sample.mla", mmap_mode='r+')  
image[10:20, 50:60] *= 5  # Modify crop in memory and disk

# read/write, partial access, create/overwrite
array = np.random.random((128, 256, 256))
image = MLArray.create("sample.mla", shape=array.shape, dtype=array.dtype, mmap_mode='w+')
image[...] = array  # Modify image in memory and disk

docs.title: Fast reading
docs.text: MLArray.open reads lazily: image[...] decompresses only the chunks a patch touches. The first open in a process also turns on blosc2's read-ahead (4 threads), which fetches those chunks in parallel and makes reads of data not in the page cache several times faster, especially on network storage. Change it with mlarray.set_read_ahead(n) (0 turns it off) or the BLOSC_PREFETCH environment variable. Files are written with nnU-Net's layout and compression settings; see ML Optimization for details.

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Metadata is explicit and domain-neutral: what each axis is, where the array sits in physical space, what its values mean, optional domain profiles, and your own metadata. Geometry is never implied: spacing, origin and direction always refer to a declared space.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((64, 128, 128))
image = MLArray(
    array,
    axes=["z", "y", "x"],
    spacing=(1.5, 1.0, 1.0),          # per array axis, in array order
    origin=(10.0, 10.0, 30.0),        # centre of index (0, 0, 0)
    direction=[[0, 0, 1], [0, 1, 0], [1, 0, 0]],  # column c: unit vector of array axis c
    space="patient",                  # DICOM patient frame (LPS)
    values={"kind": "measurement", "unit": "hounsfield_unit"},
    user={"patient_id": "123"},       # any metadata of your own
)

print(image.spacing)         # (1.5, 1.0, 1.0)
print(image.letter_codes())  # ('S', 'P', 'L')
image.set_geometry(spacing=(1.5, 5.3, 1.0))
image.user["study_id"] = "study-001"
image.save("with-metadata.mla")

# Open memory-mapped
image = MLArray.open("with-metadata.mla", mmap_mode='r+')
image.user["study_id"] = "new-study"  # Modify metadata
image.close()  # Close and save metadata, only necessary to save modified metadata

Segmentations, ML profiles and derived images:

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

base = MLArray("with-metadata.mla")
seg = MLArray(
    np.zeros(base.shape, dtype=np.uint8),
    copy=base,  # geometry, values, profiles and user metadata of base (never its source)
    values={"kind": "label", "labels": {"0": {"name": "background"}, "1": {"name": "liver"}}},
    profiles={"ml": {"split": "train"}},
)
seg.save("seg.mla")

See Usage and Schema for the full metadata model.

docs.title: Patch size variants
docs.text:
Default patch size (192): 

from mlarray import MLArray

image = MLArray("sample.mla")  # Existing file
image.save("default-patch.mla")  # Keeps existing layout metadata

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size='default')
image.save("default-patch-relayout.mla")  # Uses constructor patch_size='default' (192)

Custom isotropic patch size (512): 

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=512)
image.save("patch-512.mla")

Custom non-isotropic patch size: 

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=(128, 192, 256))
image.save("patch-non-iso.mla")

Manual chunk/block size: 

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(
    loaded.to_numpy(),
    patch_size=None,
    chunk_size=(1, 128, 128),
    block_size=(1, 32, 32),
)
image.save("manual-chunk-block.mla")

Let Blosc2 itself configure chunk/block size: 

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=None)
# If patch_size, chunk_size and block_size are all None, Blosc2 will auto-configure chunk and block size
image.save("blosc2-auto.mla")

docs.title: mlarray_convert
docs.text:
Convert between MLArray and NIfTI, NRRD, MetaImage, MGH/MGZ and DICOM with MedVol 1.0 or newer (pip install "mlarray[all]"). Nothing is reoriented, rescaled or dropped silently: the array keeps its stored order and dtype, the geometry is taken from the file's own fields, the original header is kept in source so the file can be written back faithfully, and every choice is reported.

mlarray_convert sample.nii.gz sample.mla
mlarray_convert sample.mla roundtrip.nii.gz
mlarray_convert dicom_dir/ ct.mla --dicom-tilt exact
mlarray_convert ct.mla out_dir/ --target-format dicom      # re-emits the original DICOM series

Ambiguities are resolved by explicit MedVol policies, e.g. --nifti-form sform when a NIfTI's qform and sform disagree, or --world-frame ras to store the patient space in RAS instead of DICOM's LPS.

Bases: MLArrayConstructors

Create an MLArray from an array, or load a ".mla" file.

The MLArray file format (".mla") is a Blosc2-compressed array with explicit, domain-neutral metadata (spec docs/design/spec.md).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default array Optional[Union[ndarray, str, Path]]

A NumPy array, or the path of a ".mla" file to load. None creates an instance without array data.

None axes Optional[Sequence[Union[Axis, str, Mapping]]]

One entry per array axis, in array order: names ("z"), :class:~mlarray.metadata.Axis objects or dicts with name, type (space, time, channel, component, other) and optional labels or sampling. Defaults to axis_0, axis_1, ... of type space.

None spaces Optional[Sequence[Union[Space, Mapping]]]

Coordinate systems with their from-array transform (:class:~mlarray.metadata.Space or dicts). The first space is the default one.

None values Optional[Union[Values, Mapping]]

What the numbers mean (:class:~mlarray.metadata.Values or a dict with kind, unit, labels ...).

None profiles Optional[Mapping]

Domain metadata by profile name, e.g. {"ml": {...}}.

None user Optional[Mapping]

Arbitrary user metadata; never interpreted.

None source Optional[Sequence[Union[SourceEntry, Mapping]]]

Original metadata of converted files (read-only afterwards).

None spacing, origin, direction

Convenience geometry, composed into the from-array matrix of space (see :func:mlarray.metadata.space_from_geometry). They follow the array's space axes in array order: spacing[c] and direction[:, c] belong to array axis c; origin is the centre of index (0, ..., 0) in space coordinates.

required space Optional[Union[str, Mapping, Space]]

The space the convenience geometry lives in: a preset ("patient": DICOM patient frame, LPS, millimeter) or a space description without from_array. Required with spacing, origin or direction.

None meta Optional[Union[Meta, Mapping]]

Complete metadata (:class:~mlarray.metadata.Meta or its dict form) to start from; it is copied.

None copy Optional[MLArray]

Another MLArray to take metadata from: axes, spaces, values, profiles and user, but not its history, its ml statistics and boxes, nor its source (unless copy_source=True).

None copy_source bool

Also copy the source of copy.

False patch_size Optional[Union[int, List, Tuple]]

Patch size hint for chunk/block optimization. Use "default" to use the default patch size of 192.

'default' chunk_size Optional[Union[int, List, Tuple]]

Explicit chunk size. Cannot be combined with an explicit patch_size.

None block_size Optional[Union[int, List, Tuple]]

Explicit block size. Cannot be combined with an explicit patch_size.

None cparams Optional[Union[Dict, CParams]]

Blosc2 compression parameters used when creating in-memory compressed array data.

None dparams Optional[Union[Dict, DParams]]

Blosc2 decompression parameters used for chunk access.

None compressed bool

Keep the data Blosc2-compressed in memory (default) or as a NumPy array.

True

docs.title: comp_blosc2_params classmethod
docs.text:
comp_blosc2_params(image_size: Tuple[int, ...], patch_size: Tuple[int, ...], spatial_axis_mask: Optional[list[bool]] = None, bytes_per_pixel: int = 4, max_block_nbytes: int = _layout.DEFAULT_MAX_BLOCK_NBYTES, max_chunk_nbytes: int = _layout.DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNK_NBYTES)

Compute recommended Blosc2 chunk and block sizes from a patch-size hint.

Uses nnU-Net's layout heuristic, generalized to any number of spatial and non-spatial axes (:func:mlarray.blosc2_layout_strategies.comp_blosc2_params):

1. Non-spatial axes (channels, time, ...) get chunk and block
   size 1, so reading one channel touches only its own data.
2. Blocks start at the next power of two of the patch size per
   spatial axis and are halved until they fit ``max_block_nbytes``
   (128 KiB).
3. Chunks grow by whole blocks on the least covered spatial axis
   until they reach ``max_chunk_nbytes`` (6 MiB), the image extent,
   or 1.5x the patch size per axis.

For 2 and 3 spatial axes the layout is identical to nnU-Net's.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default image_size Tuple[int, ...]

Full array shape.

required patch_size Tuple[int, ...]

Patch size over spatial axes only. A 1 keeps that axis at chunk size 1 (e.g. (1, 256, 256) for 2D slices of a 3D image).

required spatial_axis_mask Optional[list[bool]]

Mask indicating for every array axis whether it is spatial. If omitted, all axes are treated as spatial.

None bytes_per_pixel int

Number of bytes per element. Defaults to 4 for float32.

4 max_block_nbytes int

Largest block in bytes.

DEFAULT_MAX_BLOCK_NBYTES max_chunk_nbytes int

Largest chunk in bytes.

DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNK_NBYTES

Returns:

Type Description

Tuple[List[int], List[int]]: Recommended chunk size and block size.

Create a new MLArray file with memory mapping.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default filepath Union[str, Path]

Target file path. Must end with ".mla".

required shape Union[List, Tuple, ndarray]

Shape of the array to create. If provided, a new file is created. Length must match the full array dimensionality (including non-spatial axes if present).

required dtype dtype

Numpy dtype for a newly created array.

required meta Optional[Union[Meta, Mapping]]

Metadata of the created MLArray (copied), e.g. {"axes": [...], "spaces": [...]}.

None mode str

Controls storage open/creation permissions when using standard Blosc2 I/O (read-only, read/write, overwrite). Does not affect lazy loading or decompression; data is accessed and decompressed on demand by Blosc2. Must be 'w' (default). Leave at default if unsure.

'w' mmap_mode str

Controls access via OS-level memory mapping of the compressed data, including read/write permissions. Changes how bytes are fetched from disk (paging rather than explicit reads), while chunks are still decompressed on demand by Blosc2. Overrides mode if set. Must be either 'w+' (default) or None. Leave at default if unsure.

'w+' patch_size Optional[Union[int, List, Tuple]]

Patch size hint for chunk/block optimization. Provide an int for isotropic sizes or a list/tuple with length equal to the number of spatial dimensions. Use "default" to use the default patch size of 192.

'default' chunk_size Optional[Union[int, List, Tuple]]

Explicit chunk size. Provide an int or tuple/list with length equal to the array dimensions. Cannot be combined with an explicit patch_size.

None block_size Optional[Union[int, List, Tuple]]

Explicit block size. Provide an int or tuple/list with length equal to the array dimensions. Cannot be combined with an explicit patch_size.

None cparams Optional[Union[Dict, CParams]]

Blosc2 compression parameters used when creating/writing array data (for example codec, compression level, and filters). Controls how data is compressed when stored. If None, defaults to {'codec': blosc2.Codec.LZ4HC, 'clevel': 5, 'nthreads': 4} with blosc2's default filter (SHUFFLE); the data is not known yet, so no filter is chosen from it.

None dparams Optional[Union[Dict, DParams]]

Blosc2 decompression parameters used when reading/accessing compressed chunks (for example number of decompression threads). Controls runtime decompression behavior. If None, defaults to {'nthreads': 1}.

None

docs.text:
set_read_ahead(nthreads: int = MLARRAY_DEFAULT_READ_AHEAD) -> int

Set blosc2's read-ahead for this process (blosc2.set_prefetch).

With read-ahead, reading a slice of an on-disk array fetches the chunks it needs with nthreads background threads in parallel, instead of one small request after another. For data that is not in the page cache this makes patch reads several times faster, most on network storage (in our benchmark with 12 nnU-Net-style loader processes on network storage, 3D patches took 64-82% less time). For data already in the page cache it can cost a little (up to about 17% per read with a single reader).

MLArray turns it on with MLARRAY_DEFAULT_READ_AHEAD (4) threads the first time a file is opened, unless this function was called before or the BLOSC_PREFETCH environment variable is set. The setting applies to the whole process, including other blosc2 arrays it reads; each reader thread gets its own read-ahead threads. Call set_read_ahead(0) to turn it off. Without read-ahead support in the installed blosc2 this does nothing.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default nthreads int

Read-ahead threads per slice being read; 0 turns read-ahead off.

MLARRAY_DEFAULT_READ_AHEAD

Returns:

Name Type Description int int

The previous number of read-ahead threads (0 if unsupported).

docs.text:
comp_blosc2_params(image_size: Sequence[int], patch_size: Sequence[int], spatial_axis_mask: Optional[Sequence[bool]] = None, bytes_per_pixel: int = 4, max_block_nbytes: int = DEFAULT_MAX_BLOCK_NBYTES, max_chunk_nbytes: int = DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNK_NBYTES, max_chunk_to_patch_ratio_per_axis: Optional[float] = DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNK_TO_PATCH_RATIO, grow_singleton_patch_axes: bool = False) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]

Chunk and block sizes for patch-wise reading (nnU-Net's heuristic).

  • Non-spatial axes (channels, time, ...) get chunk and block size 1, so reading one channel touches only its own data.
  • Blocks start at the next power of two of the patch per spatial axis and are halved on the axis most over-represented relative to its target extent until they fit max_block_nbytes.
  • Chunks grow by whole blocks on the least covered spatial axis until max_chunk_nbytes, the image extent, or max_chunk_to_patch_ratio_per_axis times the patch per axis.
  • A patch entry of 1 (e.g. (1, 256, 256) for 2D slices of a 3D image) keeps that axis at 1 unless grow_singleton_patch_axes is set.

For 2 and 3 spatial axes the result equals nnU-Net's comp_blosc2_params (2D images as (1, y, x)); any other number of spatial axes follows the same rules.

Patch size over the spatial axes (one entry per spatial axis).

Bytes per array element.

Largest block in bytes.

Largest chunk in bytes.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
MLArray includes a small command-line interface for common tasks such as inspecting file headers and converting between MLArray and existing image formats. This is especially useful when you want to quickly verify metadata, debug a dataset, or batch-convert files without writing Python code.

The CLI currently focuses on core workflows (header inspection and conversion). Support for converting a wider range of image formats will be added over time.

docs.title: mlarray_header
docs.text:
Print the metadata of a .mla file as JSON, without loading the array.

mlarray_header sample.mla                    # core metadata: axes, spaces, values, profiles, history, storage
mlarray_header sample.mla --source --user    # also the original metadata of converted files and user metadata

The output is strict JSON (jq accepts it): non-finite numbers are printed as the strings "NaN", "Infinity" and "-Infinity", and binary values as "<binary, N bytes>".

docs.title: mlarray_convert
docs.text:
Convert between MLArray (.mla) and NIfTI (.nii, .nii.gz, .hdr/.img), NRRD (.nrrd, .nhdr), MetaImage (.mha, .mhd), MGH/MGZ and DICOM. Conversion is done by MedVol 1.0 or newer; install it with pip install "mlarray[all]".

mlarray_convert sample.nii.gz sample.mla
mlarray_convert sample.mla roundtrip.nii.gz
mlarray_convert dicom_dir/ ct.mla
mlarray_convert ct.mla out_dir/ --target-format dicom

What a conversion guarantees (MedVol spec):

  • The array keeps its stored values, dtype and storage order. Nothing is reoriented or rescaled; scaling such as NIfTI scl_slope or DICOM RescaleSlope becomes values.scale/offset.
  • The geometry comes from the file's own fields and is stored as an explicit space (DICOM patient frame, LPS, by default; --world-frame ras for RAS). Voxel positions agree between input and output to the formats' precision.
  • The original header is kept, readable, in source. Converting back to the same format reproduces it; other formats get only the fields they can represent.
  • Every ambiguity is an explicit policy, and every choice, warning and dropped field is printed and stored in the file's history.

Policy flags (defaults first): --nifti-form {nibabel,sform,qform,itk}, --nifti-form-disagreement {warn,error,ignore}, --nifti-no-codes {error,spec,nibabel,itk}, --world-frame {dicom_patient,ras}, --dicom-tilt {exact,resample,error}, --dicom-irregular-spacing {error,split,resample}, --dicom-stacks {split,largest,error}, --vector-frame {from_file,lps,ras,error}, --on-loss {warn,error}, --layout {source,default}; --source-format and --target-format name a format that cannot be detected.

docs.title: ML Optimization
docs.text:
MLArray is designed around a simple goal: make training-time I/O fast and predictable, especially for large N-D images where reading full volumes is impractical. Most ML pipelines repeatedly sample small patches/crops (e.g., nnU-Net-style random patch sampling) and the storage layout should match that access pattern.

To achieve this, MLArray builds on Blosc2 ND arrays, which store data in a two-level tiled layout:

  • Chunks: the unit stored on disk and fetched from storage.
  • Blocks: the unit decompressed; a read decompresses only the blocks it touches.

On top of that, MLArray supports memory-mapped access via Blosc2, so reading image[x0:x1, y0:y1, ...] touches only the required on-disk regions, instead of loading the whole array.

MLArray's defaults come from a benchmark of nnU-Net-style patch loading on a compute cluster (random patches, 1 to 12 loader processes, network and node-local storage, data in and not in the page cache, several datasets). In short: nnU-Net's layout and codec, mmap_mode='r' and blosc2's read-ahead were as fast as every alternative we tested, and they write fastest.

docs.title: Patch-size-driven layout
docs.text:
You tell MLArray the patch size you expect to sample during training (e.g., 192³), and it derives chunk_size and block_size with nnU-Net's heuristic, generalized to any number of axes:

  1. Non-spatial axes (channels, time, ...: every axis whose type in axes is not space) get chunk and block size 1, so reading one channel touches only its own data.
  2. Blocks start at the next power of two of the patch size per spatial axis and are halved until they fit 128 KiB.
  3. Chunks grow by whole blocks on the least covered axis until they reach 6 MiB, the image extent, or 1.5x the patch size per axis.
  4. A patch entry of 1 (e.g. (1, 256, 256) for 2D slices of a 3D image) keeps that axis at chunk size 1.

For 2D and 3D images the layout is identical to nnU-Net's. In the benchmark, smaller chunks (1.5 MiB) with LZ4HC level 9 read 4-10% faster than nnU-Net's files without read-ahead; with read-ahead the difference was gone (within 2 points), while they wrote up to 3x slower.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text: By default MLArray compresses with LZ4HC level 5 and 4 compression threads, and chooses the filter per array as nnU-Net does: it compresses a centered chunk-sized slab with and without SHUFFLE and keeps the better one (resampled intensities usually favour SHUFFLE, integer-valued ones no filter). Without data to look at (MLArray.create, empty, ...), blosc2's default SHUFFLE applies. Pass cparams to use anything else, e.g. {"codec": blosc2.Codec.ZSTD, "clevel": 5} for smaller, slower-to-read archives.

docs.title: Reading: memory mapping and read-ahead
docs.text:
• mmap_mode='r' (the default of MLArray.open) with 1 decompression thread per reader. With read-ahead on, plain reads (mmap_mode=None) were no faster for uncached data and slower for cached data.
  • Read-ahead: the first MLArray.open in a process turns on blosc2's read-ahead with 4 threads (blosc2.set_prefetch(4)). Reading a slice then fetches all chunks it needs in parallel instead of one small request after another. In the benchmark, with 12 loader processes reading 3D patches that were not in the page cache from network storage, this cut the time per read by 64-82% (3-5x faster), for larger-than-memory datasets by about 70-78% in every epoch. Reader threads in one process each get their own read-ahead threads, so threaded readers gain as much as processes.
  • For data already in the page cache, read-ahead costs a little: about 0-8% per patch with 12 processes and up to about 17% with a single reader.
  • Change or turn it off with mlarray.set_read_ahead(n) (0 = off) before opening files, or set the BLOSC_PREFETCH environment variable, which MLArray leaves alone. The setting applies to the whole process. It needs a blosc2 with read-ahead support (blosc2.set_prefetch); with older versions nothing changes.

docs.title: When should I care?
docs.text:
• If you train with patch sampling (most medical imaging pipelines do): set patch_size.
  • If you do mostly full-volume reads: patch sizing matters less; larger chunks may be fine.
  • If you have a very specific access pattern or hardware constraint: set chunk_size / block_size manually.

docs.title: Usage patterns
docs.text: Below are common end-to-end workflows. The examples show the important knobs and what they do.

docs.title: 1) “Just do the right thing” (recommended)
docs.text:
Use the default patch size optimization. If you don’t specify anything, MLArray uses an isotropic default patch size of 192 (per spatial axis) and derives chunk/block sizes automatically.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((128, 256, 256))
image = MLArray(array)

# Uses patch_size='default' (192) -> auto-derives chunk/block sizes
image.save("default-opt.mla")

When to use:

  • you want good performance without tuning,
  • your training patch size is close to ~192 (common in many 3D pipelines).

docs.title: 2) Optimize explicitly for your training patch size
docs.text:
If you know your sampler will draw patches of a specific size, set patch_size accordingly. This makes the on-disk layout match your training-time reads more closely.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((128, 256, 256))
image = MLArray(array, patch_size=(128, 192, 256))

# Optimize storage layout for 3D patches of 128×192×256 (spatial axes)
image.save("patch-non-iso.mla")

When to use:

  • your patch sampling is strongly anisotropic (common with anisotropic spacing),
  • you have a fixed patch size in your training config and want to match it.

docs.title: 3) Memory-mapped patch reads (training-style access)
docs.text:
For large files, you typically want mmap reads so random patches don’t require loading the entire array into RAM.

from mlarray import MLArray

# read-only mmap: fast random access without loading the full volume
image = MLArray.open("patch-non-iso.mla", mmap_mode='r')

patch = image[10:20, 50:60]  # Read a crop/patch (partial read)

When to use:

  • dataset is too large to fit in RAM,
  • you do random access reads (patch sampling, interactive slicing).

docs.title: 4) Memory-mapped in-place modification (advanced)
docs.text:
You can modify regions in-place with mmap_mode='r+'. This is useful for workflows like:

  • writing derived arrays (e.g., post-processing outputs),
  • patch-wise updates,
  • annotation edits (careful with concurrency).
from mlarray import MLArray

image = MLArray.open("patch-non-iso.mla", mmap_mode='r+')
image[10:20, 50:60] *= 5  # Modify crop in memory and on disk
image.close()

docs.title: 5) Create a new memory-mapped file (streaming write)
docs.text:
If you want to create a file on disk and then fill it (without holding the full array in memory), use create(..., shape=..., dtype=..., mmap_mode='w+'). MLArray will compute and store the optimized layout up front.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

shape = (128, 256, 256)
dtype = np.float32

image = MLArray.create(
    "streamed-write.mla",
    shape=shape,
    dtype=dtype,
    mmap_mode='w+',
    patch_size=192,  # optimize for your training patch size
)

# Fill incrementally if you want (here we write everything at once)
image[...] = np.random.random(shape).astype(dtype)
image.close()

When to use:

  • you generate data on the fly,
  • you want to avoid a full in-memory intermediate array.

docs.title: 6) Manual chunk/block sizing (experts only)
docs.text:
If you already know what you’re doing (or want to reproduce a very specific layout), you can override the automatic optimization. Note that in MLArray, patch_size and chunk_size/block_size are mutually exclusive.

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(
    loaded.to_numpy(),
    patch_size=None,
    chunk_size=(1, 128, 128),
    block_size=(1, 32, 32),
)
image.save("manual-layout.mla")

When to use:

  • you benchmarked and found a better layout for your hardware/access pattern,
  • you need strict reproducibility across environments.

docs.title: 7) Let Blosc2 auto-configure chunk/block sizes
docs.text:
If you set patch_size=None (and don’t provide chunk/block sizes), Blosc2 will choose chunk/block sizes itself. This can be useful for experimentation or as a baseline.

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=None)

# If patch_size, chunk_size and block_size are all None, Blosc2 auto-configures
image.save("blosc2-auto.mla")

When to use:

  • you want to compare MLArray’s layout against Blosc2 defaults,
  • you don’t have a meaningful patch size (non-ML access patterns).

docs.title: Notes and practical tips
docs.text:
• Patch optimization works for any number of spatial and non-spatial axes; for 2D and 3D images it gives nnU-Net's layout. You can still set chunk_size/block_size manually or let Blosc2 decide.
  • Reading from network storage or datasets larger than RAM: keep read-ahead on (the default). If your data always fits in RAM and is read many times by a single process, mlarray.set_read_ahead(0) can save a few percent per read.
  • The best patch size to use is usually the patch size your dataloader requests most often (training patch, not necessarily inference tile size).
  • If you’re unsure: start with the default (patch_size='default') and only tune if profiling shows I/O bottlenecks.

docs.title: MLArray Metadata Schema
docs.text: This page describes the metadata stored in an .mla file (format version 1). The normative definition is the v1 specification and the JSON Schemas shipped with the package (mlarray/schemas/mlarray-1.0.json, profile-ml-1.0.json, profile-medical-1.0.json).

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
An .mla file is a blosc2 NDArray. Its metadata lives in three blosc2 vlmeta keys, each a msgpack map that blosc2 compresses separately:

key content read mlarray version, writer, axes, spaces, values, profiles, history, storage on open mlarray.source {"source": [...]}, original metadata of converted files on first access mlarray.user {"user": {...}}, arbitrary user metadata on first access
  • Only plain msgpack types are stored: maps, arrays, strings, integers, floats, booleans, nil, binary. Nothing is pickled, and readers decode the raw bytes with plain msgpack, never through blosc2's own vlmeta decoder.
  • Opening a file reads only the mlarray key, so it stays fast however large source is.
  • Unknown keys are kept and written back at every level.
  • Files written by MLArray before v1 are not readable; convert them again from their original files.

Inspect a file with mlarray_header file.mla (add --source and --user for the lazy keys).

docs.title: version and writer
docs.text:
version: "1.0"            # metadata format version; readers accept any 1.x
writer: "mlarray 1.0.0"   # software that wrote the file

docs.title: axes
docs.text:
One entry per array axis, in array (C) order. Required.

field meaning name unique name, e.g. z, y, x, t, c. A name only: it says nothing about direction. Defaults: axis_0, axis_1, ... type space · time · channel · component · other labels one label per index, for categorical axes: ["T1", "T2", "FLAIR"] start, step, unit, unit_code uniform sampling of a non-space axis: coordinate of index i = start + i·step coordinates, unit, unit_code explicit coordinate per index (timestamps, b-values, wavelengths)

Space axes carry no sampling or unit here: their geometry lives in spaces.

docs.title: spaces
docs.text:
Optional. Without spaces the array lives in index space only (photos, ML tensors). Each space is a named coordinate system and the matrix that maps array indices into it:

spaces:
  - name: patient
    reference: {scheme: dicom_frame_of_reference, id: "1.2.826.0.1.3680043.8.498.1"}
    axes:
      - {name: x, unit: millimeter, unit_code: mm, increases_toward: left}
      - {name: y, unit: millimeter, unit_code: mm, increases_toward: posterior}
      - {name: z, unit: millimeter, unit_code: mm, increases_toward: superior}
    from_array:
      array_axes: [z, y, x]
      matrix:                              # rows: space axes x, y, z (+1)
        - [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.7, -170.1]         # columns: array_axes z, y, x (+ translation)
        - [ 0.0, 0.7, 0.0, -201.3]
        - [-2.5, 0.0, 0.0,  -87.0]
        - [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0,    1.0]
  • reference identifies the physical frame; two spaces are the same frame if scheme and id match.
  • increases_toward says in which direction a coordinate grows: left/right, anterior/posterior, superior/inferior, east/west, north/south, up/down. It replaces letter codes such as RAS or LPS, which mean different things in different tools. The example is the DICOM patient frame (LPS), the recommended world frame for medical images (space="patient" in the Python API).
  • from_array.matrix has one row per space axis plus [0, ..., 0, 1], and one column per entry of array_axes plus the translation. Rotations, oblique and mirrored grids and shear are allowed. Axis-aligned grids may use scale and translation (per array axis) instead.
  • An integer index is the centre of its voxel: matrix · [index, 1] is the coordinate of the voxel centre.
  • Spacing, origin, direction and letter codes are derived (MLArray.spacing, .origin, .direction, .letter_codes()), never stored.
  • Several spaces are allowed (e.g. patient and atlas); the first is the default.

docs.title: values
docs.text:
What the stored numbers mean. Defaults to {kind: measurement}.

field meaning kind measurement · label · instance · probability · vector · other unit, unit_code unit of the values, e.g. hounsfield_unit scale, offset physical value = scale · stored + offset; stored values are never pre-scaled fill value meaning "no data" labels for label kinds: map from value (as a decimal string) to {name, color, code}; code is an ontology reference {scheme, value, meaning} label_layout index (one label value per element) or channel (one channel per label)

docs.title: Units
docs.text: Units are a readable name plus an optional UCUM code. Use a name from the curated list (mlarray/schemas/units-1.0.json: nanometer ... kilometer, second, degree, hounsfield_unit, counts, percent, kelvin, arbitrary, ...); MLArray fills in unit_code for listed names. Free text is allowed when no listed unit fits.

docs.title: profiles
docs.text:
Optional, independent domain metadata. Profiles never repeat what the core states.

profiles:
  medical:
    profile_version: "1.0"
    dicom: {Modality: MR, BodyPartExamined: BRAIN, RepetitionTime: 2300}   # DICOM keywords
  ml:
    profile_version: "1.0"
    statistics: {min: -1024, max: 3071, mean: 40.2, standard_deviation: 410.0, percentiles: {"99.5": 1500}}
    boxes:
      frame: index            # "index" (array axes) or a space name (space coordinates)
      axes: [z, y, x]
      items: [{min: [10, 50, 60], max: [40, 90, 120], label: 1, score: 0.97}]
    patch_size: [128, 128, 128]
    split: train
  • medical.dicom holds curated medical metadata for files without a DICOM source, or deliberate overrides of source values. Files converted from DICOM keep their full DICOM metadata in source.
  • Profiles from third parties use a reverse-domain name (org_example_cryoem) and are kept as they are.

docs.title: history and storage
docs.text:
history:
  - {action: converted, tool: "medvol 2.0.0", time: "2026-11-06T10:12:00Z", from: nifti, warnings: [...]}
storage:
  chunk_size: [1, 256, 256]
  block_size: [1, 64, 64]
  patch_size: [128, 128, 128]
  compression: {codec: LZ4HC, level: 5, filters: [SHUFFLE]}

storage records only portable layout settings. Thread counts, typesize and similar runtime settings are never stored; they come from the library defaults (see ML Optimization). meta.storage.to_cparams() returns the recorded compression as blosc2.CParams.

docs.title: source and user
docs.text:
source keeps the original metadata of converted files readable and complete, so a converter can write the original format back. Each entry has format, files, reader, an index_map (how the stored array relates to the source file's own index order), a fingerprint (shape, dtype and hashes of the geometry and data) and the header as nested native values. It is read-only, and images derived from another image do not inherit it unless asked to (copy_source=True).

user holds any msgpack-compatible metadata of your own and is never interpreted.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
This section shows common usage patterns for creating, saving, and loading MLArray files, as well as working with memory mapping and metadata.

MLArray is designed to feel natural in Python workflows: you can construct an MLArray directly from a NumPy array, save it to disk, and later load it again with a single line. For large images, MLArray also supports memory-mapped access, allowing you to read and modify only small regions of an image without loading the full array into RAM. In addition, MLArray stores explicit metadata: what each axis is, where the array sits in physical space, what its values mean, optional domain profiles, and your own metadata.

Below are practical examples that cover the most common workflows.

docs.title: Default usage
docs.text:
The simplest workflow: create an MLArray from a NumPy array, save it to disk, and load it back later.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((128, 256, 256))
image = MLArray(array)  # Create MLArray image
image.save("sample.mla")

image = MLArray("sample.mla")  # Loads image

docs.title: Memory-mapped usage
docs.text:
Memory mapping allows you to access large arrays on disk without loading everything into memory. This is ideal for patch-based training, interactive visualization, or working with multi-GB/ TB-scale volumes.

from mlarray import MLArray
import numpy as np

# read-only, partial access (default)
image = MLArray.open("sample.mla", mmap_mode='r')  
crop = image[10:20, 50:60]  # Read crop

# read/write, partial access
image = MLArray.open("sample.mla", mmap_mode='r+')  
image[10:20, 50:60] *= 5  # Modify crop in memory and disk

# read/write, partial access, create/overwrite
array = np.random.random((128, 256, 256))
image = MLArray.create("sample.mla", shape=array.shape, dtype=array.dtype, mmap_mode='w+')
image[...] = array  # Modify image in memory and disk

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
MLArray metadata is explicit and domain-neutral (full definition: Schema and the v1 spec):

part meaning axes one entry per array axis, in array order: a name and a type (space, time, channel, component, other) spaces coordinate systems (e.g. the patient frame) and the matrix that maps array indices into each values what the numbers mean: kind (measurement, label, ...), unit, labels profiles optional domain metadata, e.g. medical (DICOM keywords) and ml (statistics, boxes, split) user arbitrary metadata of your own, never interpreted source the original metadata of converted files, read-only

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Geometry is never implied. An array without spaces lives in index space only. To place it in a physical frame, give spacing, origin and direction together with the space they refer to:

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((64, 128, 128))
image = MLArray(
    array,
    axes=["z", "y", "x"],             # names only; they say nothing about direction
    spacing=(2.5, 0.7, 0.7),          # per array axis, in array order (z, y, x)
    origin=(-170.1, -201.3, -87.0),   # centre of index (0, 0, 0) in space coordinates
    direction=[[0, 0, 1],             # column c = unit vector of array axis c in the space;
               [0, 1, 0],             # rows = space axes x, y, z
               [1, 0, 0]],
    space="patient",                  # DICOM patient frame: x to the left, y posterior, z superior (LPS)
)
image.save("sample.mla")

image = MLArray("sample.mla")
print(image.spacing)         # (2.5, 0.7, 0.7)
print(image.origin)          # (-170.1, -201.3, -87.0)
print(image.matrix())        # 4x4 from-array matrix; an integer index is a voxel centre
print(image.letter_codes())  # ('S', 'P', 'L'): the direction each array axis increases toward

spacing, origin and direction are derived from the stored matrix and are read-only. Change them with set_geometry; values you leave out are kept:

image.set_geometry(spacing=(3.0, 0.7, 0.7))

Without space= the geometry is refused, because spacing and orientation mean nothing until the frame is known. For full control, pass spaces=[...] with an explicit from_array matrix (see Schema).

docs.title: Values, profiles and user metadata
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

seg = MLArray(
    np.zeros((64, 128, 128), dtype=np.uint8),
    values={"kind": "label", "labels": {"0": {"name": "background"}, "1": {"name": "liver", "color": [221, 130, 101]}}},
    profiles={"ml": {"split": "train", "boxes": {"frame": "index", "axes": ["axis_0", "axis_1", "axis_2"],
                                                 "items": [{"min": [10, 50, 60], "max": [40, 90, 120], "label": 1}]}}},
    user={"annotator": "A", "notes": ["checked"]},
)
seg.user["study_id"] = "study-001"     # user metadata is a plain dict
seg.profiles["ml"]["split"] = "test"   # profiles too; they are validated when written
seg.save("seg.mla")

seg = MLArray.open("seg.mla")          # opening reads only the small core metadata
print(seg.values.kind, dict(seg.values.labels))
print(seg.user)                        # user and source are decoded on first access

Core parts (axes, spaces, values) are immutable values. Replace them as a whole; every change is checked against the array shape and leaves the metadata unchanged when it fails:

seg.axes = ["z", "y", "x"]   # raises: the ml boxes still refer to axis_0 ... axis_2

docs.title: Derived images
docs.text:
copy= takes the metadata of another image: geometry, values, profiles and user metadata. It does not take its history, its ml statistics and boxes, or its source (pass copy_source=True for that). The *_like constructors do the same and also drop label semantics.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

ct = MLArray("sample.mla")
prediction = MLArray(np.zeros(ct.shape, dtype=np.uint8), copy=ct, values={"kind": "label"})
empty = MLArray.zeros_like(ct)

docs.title: Non-spatial axes
docs.text:
Declare what each axis is. Only axes of type space take part in spaces and in the layout optimisation; channels, time steps and other axes get chunk size 1.

import numpy as np
from mlarray import MLArray

array = np.random.random((4, 16, 64, 64, 3))   # (time, z, y, x, channels)
image = MLArray(
    array,
    axes=[
        {"name": "t", "type": "time", "start": 0.0, "step": 1.5, "unit": "second"},
        "z", "y", "x",
        {"name": "c", "type": "channel", "labels": ["T1", "T2", "FLAIR"]},
    ],
    spacing=(1.0, 0.8, 0.8),   # for the space axes z, y, x
    space="patient",
)
image.save("multi-axis.mla")

docs.title: Patch size variants
docs.text: MLArray stores arrays in a chunked layout to enable efficient partial reads. You can control how data is chunked using patch_size (recommended in most cases), or manually specify chunk and block sizes when you need full control.

docs.title: Default patch size (192)
docs.text:
Uses the default patch configuration, optimized for typical ML patch-based access patterns.

from mlarray import MLArray

image = MLArray("sample.mla")
image.save("default-patch.mla")  # Keeps existing layout metadata

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size='default')
image.save("default-patch-relayout.mla")  # Uses constructor patch_size='default' (192)

docs.title: Custom isotropic patch size (512)
docs.text:
A larger patch size can improve throughput when you typically load large regions at once (at the cost of slightly less granular random access).

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=512)
image.save("patch-512.mla")

docs.title: Custom non-isotropic patch size
docs.text:
Non-isotropic patches are useful when one axis behaves differently (e.g., fewer slices in Z, anisotropic voxel spacing, or slice-wise training).

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=(128, 192, 256))
image.save("patch-non-iso.mla")

docs.title: Manual chunk/block size
docs.text:
For advanced use cases, you can explicitly define the chunk and block size used by the storage backend.

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(
    loaded.to_numpy(),
    patch_size=None,
    chunk_size=(1, 128, 128),
    block_size=(1, 32, 32),
)
image.save("manual-chunk-block.mla")

docs.title: Let Blosc2 itself configure chunk/block size
docs.text:
If you disable MLArray patch sizing, Blosc2 can choose chunk and block sizes automatically. This can be helpful when experimenting or when you want to rely entirely on backend heuristics.

from mlarray import MLArray

loaded = MLArray("sample.mla")
image = MLArray(loaded.to_numpy(), patch_size=None)
# If patch_size, chunk_size and block_size are all None, Blosc2 will auto-configure chunk and block size
image.save("blosc2-auto.mla")

docs.title: Why MLArray?
docs.text:
MLArray addresses a gap I repeatedly ran into over the last few years: we have excellent storage formats optimized for machine learning workloads, but no widely usable image format that combines efficient array storage with standardized, software-friendly metadata.

Projects like Zarr and Blosc2 already solve the “store large arrays efficiently” problem extremely well. However, they do not provide a standardized metadata layer for imaging. As a result, it’s difficult to integrate their file formats into common analysis and visualization tools in a meaningful and consistent way.

MLArray is designed to bridge that gap: a machine-learning-friendly array format that preserves metadata and enables a broader ecosystem of tooling around it.

docs.title: How does MLArray address this gap?
docs.text:
• A standardized, extensible metadata schema MLArray defines a metadata schema that balances standardization and flexibility: software that supports MLArray has a consistent way to access relevant metadata, while users can still attach arbitrary custom metadata when needed.

  • Preserve source metadata across conversions Users can convert images from arbitrary formats to MLArray while preserving the source metadata in a structured and reproducible way. Tools that integrate MLArray can still access metadata according to the source format’s conventions, which makes MLArray a practical alternative for ML pipelines without breaking downstream analysis or visualization workflows.

  • Machine learning–specific metadata support In addition to format-preserving metadata, MLArray includes a dedicated schema for machine-learning-relevant information, and it also supports storing dynamic metadata outside predefined schemas.

docs.title: What type of images can I store as MLArray?
docs.text:
In short: any array data.

MLArray was designed with very large N-dimensional images in mind, including:

  • medical imaging (radiology, histopathology, etc.)
  • satellite and remote sensing data
  • general scientific imaging
  • segmentation masks and label maps

Natural image data can also be stored in MLArray, but it is often unnecessary—formats like JPEG and PNG are already a strong default for many ML training pipelines.

MLArray can also store metadata-only or non-array data, such as:

  • bounding boxes
  • regression targets
  • classification results

This can be useful when you want a standardized interface for accessing these annotations and results, enabling simpler analysis and visualization in software that supports MLArray.

docs.title: How is MLArray optimized for Machine Learning / Deep Learning?
docs.text:
MLArray uses Blosc2 as its storage backend, which provides several properties that are particularly well-suited for machine learning and deep learning workloads.

For details, see: ML Optimization

docs.title: What the rework is
docs.text:
1. MLArray gets a new metadata model: domain-neutral core + profiles + readable source + user, plain msgpack, explicit geometry.
  2. MedVol becomes a faithful N:N converter built on that model.
  3. Before that, the existing storage and array code is cleaned up and its known bugs are fixed, without changing user-facing behaviour or storage optimisation.

docs.title: Working rules (from the user)
docs.text:
• Commit after every sensible, complete, working change. Use separate, focused commits per logical change.
  • Commit messages and docs must not mention AI, Claude or any assistant, and must not contain Co-Authored-By trailers.
  • Don't push unless asked.
  • No backwards compatibility with v0 .mla files and no migration code.
  • No de-identification and no other modification of metadata.
  • Functionality, user-facing usage and storage optimisation must not change in stages 1–2. Any bug fix that changes observable behaviour must be listed in §6 and confirmed by the user before it lands.
  • Invariant through all stages: tests/test_layout.py and tests/test_read_ahead.py stay unchanged and green (one agreed exception: in stage 3, test_layout.py's metadata accessors change, see §3). They pin the storage defaults:
  • the nnU-Net chunk/block heuristic in mlarray/blosc2_layout_strategies.py;
  • LZ4HC level 5 with 4 compression threads, and nnU-Net's per-array filter choice;
  • blosc2 read-ahead with 4 threads, switched on by the first MLArray.open (mlarray.set_read_ahead()).

docs.title: 5. After the stages
docs.text:
The follow-up work (consumers, MedVol release, CD notes) is tracked in docs/design/followups.md.

  • SlicerMLArray and napari-mlarray read the v1 core. napari should use the axis-order recipe from KB ch06 §6.3 for correct on-screen orientation.
  • Pyramids (spec §4.6, storage still to design) and lazy or streaming IO are later versions.
  • Non-medical format plugins (OME-TIFF, FITS, GeoTIFF) are later; the model already covers them (spec §5.3).

docs.title: MLArray v1 — format and metadata specification (draft)
docs.text:
Status: draft for discussion, not implemented. Branch rework/v1. Last update: 2026-11-06. Companion spec: MedVol v2 converter (medvol repo, branch rework/v2, docs/design/spec.md).

Keywords MUST, SHOULD and MAY are normative. Everything marked informative is explanation.

docs.title: 1. Goals and non-goals
docs.text:
Goals

  1. One array format for scientific images of any domain: medical, digital pathology, microscopy, astronomy, earth observation, physics, biology, natural images.
  2. A metadata model that is small, explicit and readable, with optional domain depth and room for arbitrary metadata.
  3. Geometry that cannot be misread. Every convention that has historically caused bugs is stated in the file, never implied: array axis order, world frame, axis direction, voxel centre. (Evidence: ~/projects/image-orientation-kb.)
  4. Faithful round trips. Converting format X → MLArray → X (via MedVol) reproduces X's metadata and array, to the accuracy expected of a file format (§9).
  5. Fast access: metadata needed to use the array loads in about a millisecond, and large original metadata loads only on demand (§3).

Non-goals

  • De-identification or any other modification of metadata. Metadata is stored as given.
  • Backwards compatibility with v0 files. There is no migration; v0 files must be re-converted from their sources.
  • Reading or writing other formats inside mlarray. That is MedVol's job. mlarray depends on numpy, blosc2, msgpack and xxhash only.

docs.title: 2. Terminology (informative)
docs.text:
Term Meaning array axis one dimension of the stored array, in memory order (array.shape order, C order, last axis fastest) index integer position along the array axes; index (0,…,0) is the first element space a named physical or reference coordinate system: patient, microscope stage, slide, sky, map projection, … from-array transform the mapping from array index to coordinates in one space core metadata every MLArray reader must understand (§4) profile optional, versioned domain metadata (§5) source the original metadata of the file(s) the array was converted from (§6)

Style rules for all keys and vocabulary. snake_case, full English words, no abbreviations except id, and no domain jargon in the core. Terms are chosen so that a pathologist, an astronomer and a radiologist read them the same way.

docs.title: 3. Container
docs.text:
• An .mla file is a blosc2 NDArray file (the array payload) with metadata in blosc2 variable-length metadata (vlmeta).
  • Metadata is stored in three vlmeta keys. Each value is a msgpack map, written through blosc2, which serialises with msgpack and compresses each key separately:
key content loaded mlarray version, axes, spaces, values, profiles, history, storage on open (small) mlarray.source source (§6), may be very large on first access mlarray.user user (§7), arbitrary, may be very large on first access
  • Metadata MUST NOT use pickle or any other executable serialisation.
  • Readers MUST read each key as raw bytes and decode them with plain msgpack, never through blosc2's own vlmeta decoder. That decoder can rebuild Python objects and only defaults to a safe mode in recent blosc2 versions (review finding C2, branch review/findings).
  • Values MUST be msgpack-native types: map, array, string, integer, float, boolean, nil, binary. Map key order is preserved.
  • A file always holds an array. Metadata without array data is saved as an empty array of shape (0,) * len(axes), so len(axes) == array.ndim holds for every file.

Informative. Benchmark (blosc2 4.14.1, 2026-11-06), synthetic DICOM-like headers:

original headers blosc2 metadata on disk open file read mlarray key read mlarray.source key current gzip+pickle 300 slice headers, 0.58 MB 0.30 MB 0.2 ms 0.8 ms 6.5 ms 155 ms 3000 slice headers, 5.85 MB 3.02 MB 0.5 ms 0.8 ms 55 ms 1793 ms

Opening the file stays well under 1 ms whatever the size of the source metadata. The test data was random, so real headers compress better than the ~2× shown.

docs.title: 4.1 version
docs.text:
version: "1.0"            # metadata spec version (semver). Required.
writer: "mlarray 1.0.0"   # software that wrote the file. Required.

Readers MUST accept any 1.x and MUST keep keys they don't know when rewriting a file.

docs.title: 4.2 axes — the array axes
docs.text:
One entry per array axis, in array order. len(axes) == array.ndim. Required.

field required meaning name yes unique name of the array axis, e.g. z, y, x, t, c. A name only: it says nothing about direction in space. type yes space · time · channel · component (vector or tensor components) · other (any other categorical or indexed axis: echo, b-value, batch, …) labels no one label per index for categorical axes: ["T1", "T2", "FLAIR"], ["red", "green", "blue"] start, step, unit, unit_code no uniform sampling of a non-space axis: coordinate of index i = start + i·step in unit (§4.5), e.g. time in seconds coordinates, unit, unit_code no explicit coordinate per index for non-uniform sampling: timestamps, b-values, wavelengths

Space axes carry no spacing or unit here. Their geometry lives in spaces (§4.3), so it has exactly one source of truth.

docs.title: 4.3 spaces — coordinate systems and how the array sits in them
docs.text:
Optional. Without spaces the array lives in index space only, which is valid for photos, ML tensors and the like.

spaces:
  - name: patient
    reference: {scheme: dicom_frame_of_reference, id: "1.2.826.0.1.3680043.8.498.1"}
    axes:
      - {name: x, unit: millimeter, increases_toward: left}
      - {name: y, unit: millimeter, increases_toward: posterior}
      - {name: z, unit: millimeter, increases_toward: superior}
    from_array:
      array_axes: [z, y, x]
      matrix:                              # rows: space axes x, y, z (+1)
        - [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.7, -170.1]         # columns: array_axes z, y, x (+ translation)
        - [ 0.0, 0.7, 0.0, -201.3]
        - [-2.5, 0.0, 0.0,  -87.0]
        - [ 0.0, 0.0, 0.0,    1.0]
field required meaning name yes unique space name, chosen freely (patient, stage, slide, sky, atlas, map) reference no identifies the physical frame, so files can be compared: {scheme, id}. Two spaces are the same frame iff scheme and id are equal. Examples: dicom_frame_of_reference, atlas (MNI152NLin2009cAsym), epsg (32632), celestial (ICRS) axes yes the space's own axes, in order: name, unit (+ unit_code, §4.5), optional increases_toward from_array yes how array indices map into this space (below)

increases_toward gives the direction in which a coordinate grows, as a plain word from a vocabulary: - medical: left / right / anterior / posterior / superior / inferior; - earth observation: east / west / north / south / up / down; - profiles may add more.

It replaces letter codes such as RAS/LPS/RAI, whose meaning differs between tools. The example above is the DICOM patient frame (LPS). Libraries MAY derive letter codes for display, but they MUST NOT store them.

from_array rules: 1. array_axes lists the array axes that map into this space, by name, in the order of the matrix columns. Each listed axis must have type: space. 2. matrix is a homogeneous matrix with shape (len(space.axes) + 1) × (len(array_axes) + 1). - Row r gives space coordinate r. - Column c multiplies array axis array_axes[c]. - The last column is the translation, and the last row is [0, …, 0, 1]. - Rotation, oblique axes, mirrored grids and shear (e.g. gantry-tilted CT kept exactly as acquired) are all allowed. 3. Shorthand for axis-aligned grids: scale: [...] and translation: [...] (per array axis, in array_axes order) instead of matrix. Exactly one form MUST be present. 4. An integer index is the centre of its voxel or pixel. matrix · [index, 1] is the coordinate of the voxel centre. 5. Profiles MAY define non-linear mappings (e.g. astronomy sky projections) under from_array.profile_mapping. A reader that doesn't support it still uses matrix as the linear approximation, which MUST then be present. 6. spacing, origin, direction and letter codes are derived by libraries on request and are never stored.

Several spaces are allowed, e.g. patient plus atlas after registration, or stage plus slide. The first space is the default.

docs.title: 4.4 values — what the numbers mean
docs.text:
Optional. Defaults to {kind: measurement}.

field meaning kind measurement (physical or intensity values) · label (integer class per element) · instance (integer object id per element) · probability · vector · other unit, unit_code unit of the physical value (§4.5): hounsfield_unit, counts, kelvin, reflectance, arbitrary, … scale, offset physical value = scale · stored + offset. Stored values are never pre-applied (keeps exact round trips, §9). fill value meaning "no data / outside the field of view" labels for label/instance/probability: map from value (or channel index) to {name, color, code} label_layout index (one label value per element, default) or channel (one channel per label: one-hot or probabilities, using the channel axis) 
values:
  kind: label
  labels:
    "0": {name: background}
    "1": {name: liver, color: [221, 130, 101], code: {scheme: SCT, value: "10200004", meaning: Liver}}

code is an optional ontology reference: scheme, value and human-readable meaning. For medical segmentations it carries the DICOM SEG coded concept.

docs.title: 4.5 Units
docs.text:
Wherever a unit appears (space axes, non-space axes, values), it is given as:

field meaning unit human-readable name. Writers SHOULD use a name from the curated list in mlarray/schemas/units-1.0.json; free text is allowed when no listed unit fits. unit_code optional machine-readable code in UCUM (Unified Code for Units of Measure, also used by DICOM and HL7). Writers SHOULD set it whenever it is known. The curated list gives the code for every listed name. 
{name: x, unit: millimeter, unit_code: mm, increases_toward: left}
values: {kind: measurement, unit: hounsfield_unit, unit_code: "[hnsf'U]"}

Tools compare units by unit_code when present, otherwise by unit. The curated list starts with: - SI lengths (nanometer … kilometer) and time units; - angles: degree, radian, arcsecond; - hounsfield_unit, counts, percent, kelvin, reflectance, arbitrary.

It grows through profiles.

docs.title: 4.6 Image pyramids (geometry reserved, storage not yet defined)
docs.text:
One file holds one image. The only planned exception is a multi-resolution pyramid of that same image (pathology, microscopy). Its storage layout is not part of v1. v1 only fixes how a level's geometry is described, so that the later storage design cannot reopen geometry questions:

pyramid:                      # optional, reserved. v1 readers ignore it, v1 writers do not write it
  levels:
    - level: 1
      shape: [1, 4096, 4096]
      to_base_index:          # base-array index of each element of this level
        scale: [1, 2, 2]      #   base_index = scale * level_index + offset
        offset: [0, 0.5, 0.5] #   0.5 = centre of a 2x2 block (averaging); 0 = nearest-sample decimation
      storage: null           # to be defined (separate blosc2 array, sub-file, ...)
  • Each level's position in every space is the space's from_array composed with to_base_index, so levels never need their own copy of the space geometry.
  • offset is explicit because producers differ. With averaging, the first level-1 pixel's centre is at base index 0.5, not 0. Ignoring that is the classic half-pixel shift between levels (KB ch07 §3).

docs.title: 5. Profiles
docs.text:
profiles:
  medical: {profile_version: "1.0", ...}
  ml:      {profile_version: "1.0", ...}
  1. A profile adds domain metadata. It MUST NOT change the meaning of core fields.
  2. Profiles are optional, independent and combinable.
  3. Readers MUST keep profiles they don't understand.
  4. Official profiles are published with the spec as JSON Schemas. Third-party profiles use a reverse-domain name (org_example_cryoem).
  5. One fact, one place:
  6. A profile MUST NOT copy what the core states (geometry, units, labels).
  7. It SHOULD NOT copy what source already contains verbatim; libraries expose source fields directly instead (§6.4).
  8. A profile field that does overlap a source field is a deliberate, explicit override. Read precedence is core > profile > source.

docs.title: 5.1 medical profile
docs.text:
Vocabulary: the DICOM data dictionary. Keys are DICOM keywords, values are plain msgpack values.

medical:
  profile_version: "1.0"
  dicom:                       # DICOM keywords not (or differently) present in source
    Modality: MR
    BodyPartExamined: BRAIN
    RepetitionTime: 2300
    EchoTime: 2.98
  • Typical use:
  • curated or user-provided medical metadata for files without a DICOM source, e.g. public NIfTI datasets;
  • deliberate overrides of DICOM source values.
  • Files converted from DICOM normally need no medical.dicom entries: their full DICOM metadata is in source, addressable by keyword.
  • Recommended world frame for medical images: the DICOM patient frame (x increases toward left, y toward posterior, z toward superior; LPS), with reference.scheme: dicom_frame_of_reference when the FrameOfReferenceUID is known. MedVol writes this by default.
  • Recommended array layout: the acquisition grid as stored by the source, in C order (no reorientation).

docs.title: 5.2 ml profile
docs.text:
ml:
  profile_version: "1.0"
  statistics: {min: -1024, max: 3071, mean: 40.2, standard_deviation: 410.0,
               percentiles: {"0.5": -1000, "99.5": 1500}}
  boxes:
    frame: index              # "index" (array axes below) or a space name (space coordinates)
    axes: [z, y, x]
    items:
      - {min: [10, 50, 60], max: [40, 90, 120], label: 1, score: 0.97}
  patch_size: [128, 128, 128]
  split: train

docs.title: 5.3 Further profiles (informative, defined later)
docs.text:
profile adds geometry usage microscopy per-channel excitation and emission wavelength, fluorophore, objective (numerical aperture, magnification, immersion) stage space, micrometer pathology stain, objective power, scanner, specimen and slide identifiers slide space, micrometer; microns per pixel = scale astronomy telescope, instrument, exposure, FITS WCS keywords sky space, non-linear projection via profile_mapping earth_observation bands (name, centre wavelength), acquisition time, sensor map space with reference.scheme: epsg natural camera and lens (EXIF subset), colour space usually none physics quantity names, solver, per-component units SI-unit space, component axis

How non-medical formats map onto the core (informative). This is the check that the model covers other domains; converters for these formats come later.

format geometry values other OME-TIFF / OME-Zarr PhysicalSizeX/Y/Z (+ unit) → scale of a stage space; NGFF scale/translation → same — channels → channel axis labels; wavelengths, objective → microscopy profile FITS linear WCS (CRPIX, CRVAL, CDELT/CD/PC, CUNIT) → matrix of a sky space. FITS pixel indices are 1-based with integer = pixel centre, so CRPIX − 1 gives the 0-based reference index. The projection (CTYPE e.g. RA---TAN) → astronomy profile_mapping BUNIT → unit; BSCALE/BZERO → scale/offset; BLANK → fill all cards verbatim in source GeoTIFF / COG ModelTransformation or ModelPixelScale + ModelTiepoint → matrix of a map space; CRS → reference: {scheme: epsg, id: ...}. PixelIsArea describes the pixel corner, so add half a pixel to reach our centre convention; PixelIsPoint is already a centre GDAL_NODATA → fill; scale/offset tags → scale/offset bands → channel axis; band wavelengths → earth_observation profile Plain TIFF / PNG / JPEG none (index space), or DPI → scale in inch/millimeter — EXIF → natural profile or source

docs.title: 6.1 Purpose and rules
docs.text:
source keeps the original metadata readable, authentic and complete, so that MedVol can write the original format back faithfully and users can inspect everything the source contained.

  1. source is read-only in the library API. To change metadata, edit the core or a profile.
  2. The core owns everything it describes. When exporting, MedVol regenerates core-owned source fields from the core: geometry, dimensions, data type, value scale/offset, units, labels. They can therefore never contradict the core. On an unchanged round trip they regenerate to the original values (§9).
  3. Data-dependent fields (e.g. NIfTI cal_min, DICOM LargestPixelValue, per-slice SliceLocation) are kept only while the array still matches the fingerprint (§6.3). Otherwise MedVol recomputes or drops them and records that in history.
  4. Images derived from another image (predictions, crops, resamples) MUST NOT inherit its source implicitly. Copying source is an explicit opt-in.
  5. Which fields are core-owned or data-dependent is defined per format in the MedVol spec, not in the file.

docs.title: 6.2 Structure
docs.text:
source:
  - format: nifti                       # nifti | nrrd | metaimage | mgh | dicom | mla | ...
    format_version: "1"
    files: ["sub-01_T1w.nii.gz"]        # original file name(s), relative, informative
    reader: {name: medvol, version: "2.0.0"}
    index_map:                          # how MLArray indices relate to the source file's own indices
      axis_order: [2, 1, 0]             # source axis feeding each MLArray axis
      flipped: [false, false, false]
      offset: [0, 0, 0]
    fingerprint: {shape: [176, 256, 256], dtype: int16, geometry: "<hash>", data: "<xxh3 hash>"}
    header: { ... readable original metadata, §6.4 ... }

index_map keeps raw geometry fields (NIfTI srow_*, DICOM ImagePositionPatient, NRRD space directions) interpretable. They refer to the source's own index order, and index_map says how that relates to the stored array.

docs.title: 6.3 Fingerprint
docs.text:
Written at conversion time: - shape and dtype; - a hash of the core geometry (axes and spaces, after rounding to the accuracy of §9); - a fast hash of the array data (xxh3).

MedVol compares it on export to decide whether data-dependent fields are still valid.

docs.title: 6.4 Readable header representation
docs.text:
The header is stored as nested maps with native types, not as raw bytes:

  • Numbers are numbers. Integers stay integers. Floats are stored as the shortest decimal value that converts back to the original binary value: a float32 0.7 is stored as 0.7, not 0.699999988079071.
  • Text is text. Fixed-length or null-padded strings are stored stripped, and MedVol re-pads on export.
  • Field order is preserved.
  • Binary content (NIfTI extensions with binary payload, DICOM OB/OW/UN elements) is stored as msgpack binary. Viewers display such values as <binary, N bytes>.
  • DICOM:
  • Public elements are keyed by keyword (Modality, ImagePositionPatient). Private elements are keyed by tag "(0029,1010)" and carry {vr, value}, because their type is not in the dictionary.
  • Sequences are lists of maps.
  • A multi-file series is stored as shared (identical in every file, stored once) plus per_file (a list with only the fields that differ, in file order) plus file_names.
  • Format-layout fields (NIfTI vox_offset, NRRD encoding, DICOM transfer syntax) are kept like any other field. MedVol reuses them on export unless told otherwise.

docs.title: 7. user
docs.text: Arbitrary msgpack-compatible metadata, never interpreted or validated by MLArray. It replaces v0's extra and lives in its own lazily loaded key.

docs.title: 8. history and storage
docs.text:
history:
  - {action: converted, tool: "medvol 2.0.0", time: "2026-11-06T10:12:00Z",
     from: nifti, settings: {nifti_form: nibabel},
     warnings: ["qform and sform disagree by 4.9 mm; used sform (sform_code=2)"]}
storage:
  chunk_size: [1, 256, 256]
  block_size: [1, 64, 64]
  patch_size: [128, 128, 128]
  compression: {codec: LZ4HC, level: 5, filters: [SHUFFLE]}

history is an append-only list of conversions and operations with tool, version, settings and warnings.

storage describes the blosc2 layout. It is an implementation detail with no scientific meaning. - It MUST contain only portable properties of the file: chunk, block and patch size, codec, level and filters. - It MUST NOT contain runtime or machine-specific settings: thread counts, typesize, internal blocksize, read-ahead (review finding M12). Those are chosen at runtime by the library defaults (docs/optimization.md: nnU-Net layout heuristic, LZ4HC-5 with 4 compression threads, read-ahead with 4 threads) or by the user per call.

docs.title: 9. Accuracy standard
docs.text:
The guarantee is "what a careful file format guarantees", not byte identity:

item guarantee array values bit-identical. Stored values are kept in the original dtype, with no rescaling or reorientation unless explicitly requested. integers, strings, booleans, binary identical floating-point header values identical binary value when the source stores binary floats (NIfTI, MGH, DICOM FL/FD). For text-encoded numbers (NRRD, MetaImage, DICOM DS/IS) the numeric value is identical, but the textual spelling may differ (0.69999999999999996 ↔ 0.7, 1.0 ↔ 1). geometry through from_array.matrix float64; round-trip error ≤ 1e-9 relative. Below every format's own precision (NIfTI srow is float32; DICOM DS has 16 characters). field order and set of fields identical for same-format round trips, except fields the format itself defines as derived (e.g. NIfTI vox_offset when the extension size changes) file bytes not guaranteed: compression level, gzip timestamps, padding and whitespace may differ

Cross-format conversion (X → MLArray → Y, Y ≠ X) preserves the core. MedVol reports which source fields Y cannot represent.

docs.title: 10. Validation
docs.text: The normative definitions are JSON Schemas shipped in the repo: mlarray/schemas/mlarray-1.0.json, mlarray/schemas/profile-medical-1.0.json, mlarray/schemas/profile-ml-1.0.json. They are installed with the package. They are applied to the msgpack content as if it were JSON, with binary allowed in source/user. The Python model implements the schemas. Third-party readers (SlicerMLArray, napari-mlarray, future C++/JS) validate against the same files.

docs.title: 11. Python API (informative sketch)
docs.text:
img = MLArray("ct.mla")                       # opens; loads key "mlarray" only
img.axes                                      # [Axis(name="z", type="space"), ...]
img.space()                                   # default space; img.space("atlas")
img.matrix()                                  # from-array matrix of the default space
img.spacing, img.origin, img.direction        # derived, read-only
img.letter_codes()                            # derived display helper, e.g. ("L","P","S"), points-to
img.values.kind, img.values.labels
img.profiles["medical"]["dicom"]
img.source                                    # lazy; read-only view
img.source[0].header["RepetitionTime"]        # DICOM keyword access
img.user                                      # lazy

MLArray(array, axes=[...], spaces=[...], values=...)        # explicit construction
MLArray(array, spacing=..., origin=..., direction=..., space="patient")  # convenience; composed into matrix
